text:
## Observations

1. Two vertices are adjacent exactly when one interval ends strictly before the other begins. If the query endpoints are adjacent, the direct path is optimal because all vertex weights are positive.
2. Every minimum-weight path has at most three edges. A chord would let the path skip positive-weight vertices, so an optimal path is chordless. A chordless path with at least four edges would have two disjoint edges with no edge between their endpoint sets, using the first two and the fourth and fifth vertices. This is impossible here. For any two disjoint edges, orient each from its left interval to its right interval. Whichever left interval ends earlier also ends strictly before the other right interval begins, giving an edge between the endpoint sets.
3. For overlapping query intervals, a common neighbor lies entirely to the left of both or entirely to the right of both.
4. A chordless three-edge path alternates between moving right and moving left. Two consecutive moves in the same direction would create a chord. For overlapping endpoints, an interval to the right of the start and an interval to the left of the target are automatically disjoint, since the latter ends before the target begins, and the target begins at or before the start ends. The same argument applies with start and target exchanged.
5. All candidate internal-vertex weights can be obtained from prefix minima indexed by right endpoint and suffix minima indexed by left endpoint. All coordinates are in the range from 1 through 2N.

## Solution sketch

1. “All candidate internal-vertex weights can be obtained from prefix minima indexed by right endpoint and suffix minima indexed by left endpoint. All coordinates are in the range from 1 through 2N.” At each coordinate, record the minimum weight of any interval ending there and the minimum weight of any interval starting there in separate arrays. Take prefix minima of the first array and suffix minima of the second. An empty minimum is infinity. Use sentinel entries at coordinates 0 and \(2N+1\) so that a lookup strictly before the smallest coordinate or strictly after the largest coordinate also gives infinity.
2. “Two vertices are adjacent exactly when one interval ends strictly before the other begins. If the query endpoints are adjacent, the direct path is optimal because all vertex weights are positive.” For each query \(s,t\), check whether \(R_s<L_t\) or \(R_t<L_s\). If either holds, print \(W_s+W_t\). Otherwise, evaluate the remaining candidates. In particular, intervals that share an endpoint count as overlapping.
3. “For overlapping query intervals, a common neighbor lies entirely to the left of both or entirely to the right of both.” For a two-edge path, look up the prefix minimum at \(\min(L_s,L_t)-1\) and the suffix minimum at \(\max(R_s,R_t)+1\). The smaller value is the minimum internal weight of a two-edge path.
4. “A chordless three-edge path alternates between moving right and moving left. Two consecutive moves in the same direction would create a chord. For overlapping endpoints, an interval to the right of the start and an interval to the left of the target are automatically disjoint, since the latter ends before the target begins, and the target begins at or before the start ends. The same argument applies with start and target exchanged.” For a right-left-right path, add the suffix minimum at \(R_s+1\) to the prefix minimum at \(L_t-1\). For a left-right-left path, add the prefix minimum at \(L_s-1\) to the suffix minimum at \(R_t+1\). The two internal vertices can be chosen independently in each case because their mutual edge is guaranteed. If either minimum is infinity, that candidate is unavailable.
5. “Every minimum-weight path has at most three edges. A chord would let the path skip positive-weight vertices, so an optimal path is chordless. A chordless path with at least four edges would have two disjoint edges with no edge between their endpoint sets, using the first two and the fourth and fifth vertices. This is impossible here. For any two disjoint edges, orient each from its left interval to its right interval. Whichever left interval ends earlier also ends strictly before the other right interval begins, giving an edge between the endpoint sets.” For an overlapping pair, take the minimum of the two-edge candidate and the two three-edge candidates. If it is finite, add \(W_s+W_t\) and print the result. Otherwise print \(-1\), since any reachable pair would have an optimal path among the cases considered.
6. “All candidate internal-vertex weights can be obtained from prefix minima indexed by right endpoint and suffix minima indexed by left endpoint. All coordinates are in the range from 1 through 2N.” Building the arrays takes \(O(N)\) time and space. Each query uses a constant number of comparisons and lookups, for \(O(N+Q)\) total time and \(O(N)\) auxiliary space when queries are processed in order.
system_prompt:
You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.
## Solution sketch
Describe one coherent algorithm as numbered steps. Before each step quote the
relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.
Cover edge cases and time/space complexity in the sketch.
Return prose only, without Python implementation or command blocks.
The guide will be implemented by a separate coding agent.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
